Remember systole means contraction and diastole means relaxation. Think about the order: atria squeeze first to fill ventricles, then ventricles squeeze to push blood out, then both relax briefly.
walkthrough:
Link Squeezing To Blood Movement**
Systole means the muscle wall contracts and raises pressure to push blood out. Diastole means the muscle relaxes and pressure falls so blood can enter. So always match the action to the blood movement described.

Apply To Boxes 3, 5 And 7**
Box 3 leads to box 4 where blood is forced into the right ventricle, so the atrium must be in systole squeezing while the ventricle is in diastole relaxing to fill. Box 5 leads to box 6 where blood leaves the ventricle for the pulmonary arteries, so the ventricle must now be in systole while the atrium is in diastole. Box 7 is after ejection, the short pause before the next fill, so both atria and ventricles are in diastole.
Final answer: Box 3: atrial systole, ventricular diastole. Box 5: atrial diastole, ventricular systole. Box 7: atrial diastole, ventricular diastole.

walkthrough:
Why Atria And Ventricles Must Not Squeeze Together**
The SAN in the right atrium starts excitation, so the atria go into systole first. If the impulse passed instantly to the ventricles, both would be in systole together and blood could not move from atrium to ventricle.

How The Delay Helps Filling**
The short delay at the AVN holds up the impulse for about 0.1 s while atrial systole finishes. That gives time for the atria to empty completely and for the ventricles to fill with blood, ready for the stronger ventricular systole that follows.

Final answer: Atria and ventricles do not contract at the same time; ventricles contract after atria. This allows the atria to empty completely and the ventricles to fill fully with blood before ventricular systole.

hints: Valves do not open by themselves. They open when pressure on one side pushes harder than on the other side. For the tricuspid valve, compare right atrium pressure with right ventricle pressure.
Now do the same for the pulmonary valve at the exit of the ventricle. Compare right ventricle pressure with pulmonary artery pressure during ventricular systole.
Step back and think about the whole heart. If blood always moves from higher to lower pressure and valves prevent backflow, how does this keep flow in one direction?
walkthrough:
Opening The Tricuspid Valve**
When the atrium is in systole or filling and the ventricle is in diastole, pressure in the right atrium becomes higher than pressure in the relaxed right ventricle. This pressure difference pushes the atrioventricular tricuspid valve open so blood flows into the ventricle.

Opening The Pulmonary Valve**
When the ventricle then goes into systole, its wall contracts and pressure in the right ventricle rises sharply. When ventricular pressure becomes higher than pressure in the pulmonary artery, the semilunar pulmonary valve is pushed open so blood is ejected.

How This Helps Flow Through The Heart**
Blood always flows from higher pressure to lower pressure. Because valves open only in response to the correct pressure gradient and then shut to prevent backflow, blood is kept moving in one direction: atrium to ventricle to pulmonary artery. The timing also coordinates the valves, so when the pulmonary valve is open the tricuspid is shut.

Final answer: Tricuspid opens when pressure in right ventricle falls below pressure in right atrium. Pulmonary opens when pressure in right ventricle rises above pressure in pulmonary artery. This ensures one-way flow from higher to lower pressure and prevents backflow, directing blood from atrium to ventricle to pulmonary artery.
